auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

tools.name: Skill

Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

- codex:codex-rescue: Proactively use when Claude Code is stuck, wants a second implementation or diagnosis pass, needs a deeper root-cause investigation, or should hand a substantial coding task to Codex through the shared runtime (Tools: Bash)
- deep-reasoner: Independent deep second opinion — a different model's perspective, uncontaminated by the orchestrator's context. Use for parallel takes on high-stakes decisions, adversarial review of a design or diagnosis, and the two-model panel pattern with Codex. For the hardest in-thread reasoning that needs full conversation context, use a fork instead. (Tools: All tools)
- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- fast-worker: Use for mechanical tasks — boilerplate, formatting, renames, simple edits, mechanical test scaffolding (adding table-driven cases, fixtures). Not for tests that require designing new behavior coverage (use coder). Execute efficiently. (Tools: All tools)
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)
- pr-review-toolkit:code-simplifier: Use this agent when code has been written or modified and needs to be simplified for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. This agent should be triggered automatically after completing a coding task or writing a logical chunk of code. It simplifies code by following project best practices while retaining all functionality. The agent focuses only on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise.

Examples:

<example>
Context: The assistant has just implemented a new feature that adds user authentication to an API endpoint.
user: "Please add authentication to the /api/users endpoint"
assistant: "I've implemented the authentication for the /api/users endpoint. Here's the code:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
Since a logical chunk of code has been written (authentication feature), use the Task tool to launch the code-simplifier agent to improve the code's clarity and maintainability while preserving functionality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now let me use the code-simplifier agent to refine this implementation for better clarity and maintainability"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just fixed a bug by adding several conditional checks.
user: "Fix the null pointer exception in the data processor"
assistant: "I've added the necessary null checks to prevent the exception:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After modifying code to fix a bug, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the fix follows best practices and maintains code quality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Let me refine this bug fix using the code-simplifier agent to ensure it follows our best practices"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just refactored a function to improve performance.
user: "Optimize the data sorting algorithm for better performance"
assistant: "I've optimized the sorting algorithm. Here's the updated implementation:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After completing a performance optimization task, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and maintainable.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now I'll use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and follows our coding standards"

See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. Examples:\n\n<example>\nContext: Daisy has just finished implementing a new feature that fetches data from an API with fallback behavior.\nDaisy: "I've added error handling to the API client. ## claude.ai Buildkite
This is the Buildkite MCP Server. It provides access to the Buildkite CI/CD API, enabling you to manage and inspect pipelines, builds, jobs, logs, clusters, tests, artifacts, and annotations.

Start here: Before using most tools, call user_token_organization to retrieve the organization slug. Nearly every other tool requires the org_slug parameter, and this call is the fastest way to discover it.

Skill discovery: Always call list_skills early in a session — it's cheap (names and one-line descriptions only) and surfaces guidance not visible in any tool's name or schema. When a task matches a listed skill, call load_skill for that guide — it covers parameter tuning, caching behavior, and details beyond the summaries below. Guides cover the full server; only follow steps for tools advertised in this session. Never call tools excluded by minimum-access mode or toolset settings.

Authorization: Tools available depend on the scopes and organization access granted to the configured API token. A 401 response means the token is invalid, expired, or revoked and requires reauthentication. A 403 response means the credentials were accepted but access was denied, commonly because the token lacks a required scope or organization access, or the user lacks permission.

Common pitfalls:

build_number is a sequential integer string (e.g. "42"), not a UUID. Build, job, artifact, and log tools all require this identifier — do not use the build's UUID id field.

Build failure investigation: start with get_build_failure_summary. It combines build state, blocking failed and canceled jobs, promised failures from running jobs, soft-failed jobs (listed after blocking failures and canceled jobs), bounded log tails, relevant annotations, and failed tests in one response; jobs that never ran (broken, waiting_failed, blocked_failed, unblocked_failed) fill the remaining max_jobs slots unless include_never_ran_jobs is false. Use the individual build, job, log, annotation, and test tools only when the summary identifies an area that needs deeper inspection.

Pipeline authoring: always check pipeline YAML with validate_pipeline before creating or updating a pipeline, or before committing changes to .buildkite/pipeline.yml. It validates against the official pipeline schema locally — the call itself never contacts the Buildkite API and works regardless of the configured token's scopes — and catches structural errors that would otherwise fail silently at upload time. A valid result does not guarantee runtime correctness (environment variable interpolation, plugin configuration, dynamically generated steps).

Build comparison: use compare_builds when asked what changed since a build worked, or to compare two builds. Without an explicit baseline it selects an earlier successful build on the same pipeline and branch. Report the selected baseline and unmatched steps; shared failing steps do not establish a shared cause or justify a retry. Timings cover final attempts, not total retry cost or build wall-clock duration.

Job state "broken" means the pipeline configuration decided, when the job was created, that it would not run: an `if` condition or `branches` filter did not match, `parallelism` was 0, or the step was marked `skip`. Broken is never caused by another job failing, never fails a build, and is normal in passing builds. Jobs stopped by a failed dependency are `waiting_failed`, `blocked_failed` or `unblocked_failed` instead; those appear only in builds that actually failed and are consequences of an upstream failure, not root causes. None of these four states ran, so they have no logs. `failed` = ran and exited non-zero; `skipped` = an external factor (e.g. a newer build superseded it). To explain a red build, investigate only `failed`, `timed_out`, `expired` jobs that are not `soft_failed`, as well as `running` jobs that have non-zero `promised_exit_status`.

Soft failures: a job with `soft_failed` true actually ran and exited unsuccessfully, but the step's `soft_fail` setting allowed that exit status, so the failure did not block the build. `soft_fa… [truncated]

## claude.ai Claude Data
The queries this organization has certified, and results its members share on artifacts. Certify, uncertify, set up or share only when a person asked for exactly that. From a certified-query tool, org_disabled means certified queries are off for this organization: do not mention them or offer to certify or set up, and say they are off only if a person asks. In a conversation, share_live_queries is only for a connector whose share is the person's own (the shares in get_live_results list it with yours true and no suspended), when they asked you to change or add a query on it, and after telling them that every viewer will see the changed results. When it is someone else's, say that its sharer must share the change, or that they can take the connector over on the artifact's page, which ends its sharer's share, and every viewer then gets results run with the person's own access. ## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. ## claude.ai Datadog
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). See Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ When `execute_code` is available, use it to read Datadog data, even for a single lookup: one script can make several API calls, join data across products, and return only what the answer needs. Skill guides still apply for domain knowledge (query syntax, attribute and metric names, pitfalls), but where a guide tells you to call a specific read tool such as `search_datadog_logs`, `analyze_datadog_logs`, or `get_datadog_metric`, make the equivalent call from `execute_code` instead, using `search_datadog_sdk` to find it. This takes precedence over tool choices in skill guides. Use the named tool only when `search_datadog_sdk` finds no operation for what you need, or when `execute_code` still fails for a step after following its own error guidance. This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Investigation results often benefit from charts.

## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (project-level units of work, each holding one PR-like Change per repository branch), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings. To create a trail for a branch, call trail_create with repo, title, body, branchName, and branchAction. For a trail web URL (…/-/trails/…), call project_trail action=get with url.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, entire/trails before trail work, entire/querying for the full querying reference. Load them proactively, at the start of the work, not after an error.

Feedback: if a tool is wrong, misleading, or missing something, call send_entire_feedback (name the tool). Code search is gated per jurisdiction — where the index is not deployed, those tools say so.

## claude.ai Linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

Tools accept human-readable references, so you rarely need to look up IDs first: issue identifiers such as LIN-123, project identifiers such as P-ENG-12, team names or keys, user names or emails, and "me" for the authenticated user. Only call list_teams, list_users, or similar tools when a reference is ambiguous or unknown.

Use list_issues for structured queries, such as the issues assigned to "me" in a team, status, label, project, or cycle, and its query parameter for keyword search. Results are paginated: when hasNextPage is true, pass the returned cursor to fetch the next page rather than assuming the first page is complete.

Statuses and labels belong to teams and differ between them. When you are not sure which values a team supports, call list_issue_statuses or list_issue_labels for that team before filtering or setting them.

get_issue does not include the issue's discussion. Call list_comments with the issue ID to read comments, including inline comments on the description.

Issue descriptions, comments, and documents often embed screenshots and other uploads as markdown images. Pass that markdown to extract_images to view them. Read issue attachments with get_attachment; files uploaded in comments are returned in the attachments field of list_comments. Linear upload URLs are signed and expire after a few minutes, so fetch them again instead of reusing old URLs.

Tools named save_* both create and update: omit id to create a new entity, or pass id to update an existing one. When updating, pass only the fields you want to change. To edit part of a long issue description or document, pass patch instead of resending the full content.

Before creating an issue, check with list_issues whether a matching issue already exists, to avoid duplicates. When creating, team is required.

The labels parameter of save_issue replaces the issue's full label set. To add or remove individual labels without dropping others, use addLabels and removeLabels instead.

Markdown content supports user mentions with @displayName (for example @johndoe). To embed an image or file, upload it with prepare_file_upload and insert the markdown it returns; do not inline base64 data.

Write issue descriptions for people to read. Keep sentences short, and use the same term for the same concept throughout.

Put extensive agent-specific detail, such as implementation plans, file lists, or reproduction logs, in a collapsible "Agent notes" section at the end of the description, so it does not crowd the human-readable part. A collapsible section opens with +++ followed by its title, and closes with +++ on its own line:

+++ Agent notes

Details for agents go here.

+++

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Buildkite
This is the Buildkite MCP Server. It provides access to the Buildkite CI/CD API, enabling you to manage and inspect pipelines, builds, jobs, logs, clusters, tests, artifacts, and annotations.

Start here: Before using most tools, call user_token_organization to retrieve the organization slug. Nearly every other tool requires the org_slug parameter, and this call is the fastest way to discover it.

Skill discovery: Always call list_skills early in a session — it's cheap (names and one-line descriptions only) and surfaces guidance not visible in any tool's name or schema. When a task matches a listed skill, call load_skill for that guide — it covers parameter tuning, caching behavior, and details beyond the summaries below. Guides cover the full server; only follow steps for tools advertised in this session. Never call tools excluded by minimum-access mode or toolset settings.

Authorization: Tools available depend on the scopes and organization access granted to the configured API token. A 401 response means the token is invalid, expired, or revoked and requires reauthentication. A 403 response means the credentials were accepted but access was denied, commonly because the token lacks a required scope or organization access, or the user lacks permission.

Common pitfalls:

build_number is a sequential integer string (e.g. "42"), not a UUID. Build, job, artifact, and log tools all require this identifier — do not use the build's UUID id field.

Build failure investigation: start with get_build_failure_summary. It combines build state, blocking failed and canceled jobs, promised failures from running jobs, soft-failed jobs (listed after blocking failures and canceled jobs), bounded log tails, relevant annotations, and failed tests in one response; jobs that never ran (broken, waiting_failed, blocked_failed, unblocked_failed) fill the remaining max_jobs slots unless include_never_ran_jobs is false. Use the individual build, job, log, annotation, and test tools only when the summary identifies an area that needs deeper inspection.

Pipeline authoring: always check pipeline YAML with validate_pipeline before creating or updating a pipeline, or before committing changes to .buildkite/pipeline.yml. It validates against the official pipeline schema locally — the call itself never contacts the Buildkite API and works regardless of the configured token's scopes — and catches structural errors that would otherwise fail silently at upload time. A valid result does not guarantee runtime correctness (environment variable interpolation, plugin configuration, dynamically generated steps).

Build comparison: use compare_builds when asked what changed since a build worked, or to compare two builds. Without an explicit baseline it selects an earlier successful build on the same pipeline and branch. Report the selected baseline and unmatched steps; shared failing steps do not establish a shared cause or justify a retry. Timings cover final attempts, not total retry cost or build wall-clock duration.

Job state "broken" means the pipeline configuration decided, when the job was created, that it would not run: an `if` condition or `branches` filter did not match, `parallelism` was 0, or the step was marked `skip`. Broken is never caused by another job failing, never fails a build, and is normal in passing builds. Jobs stopped by a failed dependency are `waiting_failed`, `blocked_failed` or `unblocked_failed` instead; those appear only in builds that actually failed and are consequences of an upstream failure, not root causes. None of these four states ran, so they have no logs. `failed` = ran and exited non-zero; `skipped` = an external factor (e.g. a newer build superseded it). To explain a red build, investigate only `failed`, `timed_out`, `expired` jobs that are not `soft_failed`, as well as `running` jobs that have non-zero `promised_exit_status`.

Soft failures: a job with `soft_failed` true actually ran and exited unsuccessfully, but the step's `soft_fail` setting allowed that exit status, so the failure did not block the build. `soft_fa… [truncated]

The queries this organization has certified, and results its members share on artifacts. Certify, uncertify, set up or share only when a person asked for exactly that. From a certified-query tool, org_disabled means certified queries are off for this organization: do not mention them or offer to certify or set up, and say they are off only if a person asks. In a conversation, share_live_queries is only for a connector whose share is the person's own (the shares in get_live_results list it with yours true and no suspended), when they asked you to change or add a query on it, and after telling them that every viewer will see the changed results. When it is someone else's, say that its sharer must share the change, or that they can take the connector over on the artifact's page, which ends its sharer's share, and every viewer then gets results run with the person's own access. Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. This takes precedence over tool choices in skill guides. Use the named tool only when `search_datadog_sdk` finds no operation for what you need, or when `execute_code` still fails for a step after following its own error guidance. ## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (project-level units of work, each holding one PR-like Change per repository branch), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings. To create a trail for a branch, call trail_create with repo, title, body, branchName, and branchAction. For a trail web URL (…/-/trails/…), call project_trail action=get with url.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, entire/trails before trail work, entire/querying for the full querying reference. Load them proactively, at the start of the work, not after an error.

Feedback: if a tool is wrong, misleading, or missing something, call send_entire_feedback (name the tool). Code search is gated per jurisdiction — where the index is not deployed, those tools say so.

## claude.ai Linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

Tools accept human-readable references, so you rarely need to look up IDs first: issue identifiers such as LIN-123, project identifiers such as P-ENG-12, team names or keys, user names or emails, and "me" for the authenticated user. Only call list_teams, list_users, or similar tools when a reference is ambiguous or unknown.

Use list_issues for structured queries, such as the issues assigned to "me" in a team, status, label, project, or cycle, and its query parameter for keyword search. Results are paginated: when hasNextPage is true, pass the returned cursor to fetch the next page rather than assuming the first page is complete.

Statuses and labels belong to teams and differ between them. When you are not sure which values a team supports, call list_issue_statuses or list_issue_labels for that team before filtering or setting them.

get_issue does not include the issue's discussion. Call list_comments with the issue ID to read comments, including inline comments on the description.

Issue descriptions, comments, and documents often embed screenshots and other uploads as markdown images. Pass that markdown to extract_images to view them. Read issue attachments with get_attachment; files uploaded in comments are returned in the attachments field of list_comments. Linear upload URLs are signed and expire after a few minutes, so fetch them again instead of reusing old URLs.

Tools named save_* both create and update: omit id to create a new entity, or pass id to update an existing one. When updating, pass only the fields you want to change. To edit part of a long issue description or document, pass patch instead of resending the full content.

Before creating an issue, check with list_issues whether a matching issue already exists, to avoid duplicates. When creating, team is required.

The labels parameter of save_issue replaces the issue's full label set. To add or remove individual labels without dropping others, use addLabels and removeLabels instead.

Markdown content supports user mentions with @displayName (for example @johndoe). To embed an image or file, upload it with prepare_file_upload and insert the markdown it returns; do not inline base64 data.

Write issue descriptions for people to read. Keep sentences short, and use the same term for the same concept throughout.

Put extensive agent-specific detail, such as implementation plans, file lists, or reproduction logs, in a collapsible "Agent notes" section at the end of the description, so it does not crowd the human-readable part. A collapsible section opens with +++ followed by its title, and closes with +++ on its own line:

+++ Agent notes

Details for agents go here.

+++

content.text:
Available agent types for the Agent tool:
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)
- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)
- coder: Use for standard, well-scoped coding tasks — implementing a designed feature, bug fixes with a known cause, endpoints, migrations, tests for new behavior, moderate refactors. More capable than fast-worker (which is for mechanical edits); not for open-ended design or gnarly debugging (those need conversation context — keep them with the orchestrator or a fork; use deep-reasoner only for an independent second opinion). (Tools: All tools)
- codex:codex-rescue: Proactively use when Claude Code is stuck, wants a second implementation or diagnosis pass, needs a deeper root-cause investigation, or should hand a substantial coding task to Codex through the shared runtime (Tools: Bash)
- deep-reasoner: Independent deep second opinion — a different model's perspective, uncontaminated by the orchestrator's context. Use for parallel takes on high-stakes decisions, adversarial review of a design or diagnosis, and the two-model panel pattern with Codex. For the hardest in-thread reasoning that needs full conversation context, use a fork instead. (Tools: All tools)
- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- fast-worker: Use for mechanical tasks — boilerplate, formatting, renames, simple edits, mechanical test scaffolding (adding table-driven cases, fixtures). Not for tests that require designing new behavior coverage (use coder). Execute efficiently. (Tools: All tools)
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. ## claude.ai Buildkite
This is the Buildkite MCP Server. It provides access to the Buildkite CI/CD API, enabling you to manage and inspect pipelines, builds, jobs, logs, clusters, tests, artifacts, and annotations.

Start here: Before using most tools, call user_token_organization to retrieve the organization slug. Nearly every other tool requires the org_slug parameter, and this call is the fastest way to discover it.

Skill discovery: Always call list_skills early in a session — it's cheap (names and one-line descriptions only) and surfaces guidance not visible in any tool's name or schema. When a task matches a listed skill, call load_skill for that guide — it covers parameter tuning, caching behavior, and details beyond the summaries below. Guides cover the full server; only follow steps for tools advertised in this session. Never call tools excluded by minimum-access mode or toolset settings.

Authorization: Tools available depend on the scopes and organization access granted to the configured API token. A 401 response means the token is invalid, expired, or revoked and requires reauthentication. A 403 response means the credentials were accepted but access was denied, commonly because the token lacks a required scope or organization access, or the user lacks permission.

Common pitfalls:

build_number is a sequential integer string (e.g. "42"), not a UUID. Build, job, artifact, and log tools all require this identifier — do not use the build's UUID id field.

Build failure investigation: start with get_build_failure_summary. It combines build state, blocking failed and canceled jobs, promised failures from running jobs, soft-failed jobs (listed after blocking failures and canceled jobs), bounded log tails, relevant annotations, and failed tests in one response; jobs that never ran (broken, waiting_failed, blocked_failed, unblocked_failed) fill the remaining max_jobs slots unless include_never_ran_jobs is false. Use the individual build, job, log, annotation, and test tools only when the summary identifies an area that needs deeper inspection.

Pipeline authoring: always check pipeline YAML with validate_pipeline before creating or updating a pipeline, or before committing changes to .buildkite/pipeline.yml. It validates against the official pipeline schema locally — the call itself never contacts the Buildkite API and works regardless of the configured token's scopes — and catches structural errors that would otherwise fail silently at upload time. A valid result does not guarantee runtime correctness (environment variable interpolation, plugin configuration, dynamically generated steps).

Build comparison: use compare_builds when asked what changed since a build worked, or to compare two builds. Without an explicit baseline it selects an earlier successful build on the same pipeline and branch. Report the selected baseline and unmatched steps; shared failing steps do not establish a shared cause or justify a retry. Timings cover final attempts, not total retry cost or build wall-clock duration.

Job state "broken" means the pipeline configuration decided, when the job was created, that it would not run: an `if` condition or `branches` filter did not match, `parallelism` was 0, or the step was marked `skip`. Broken is never caused by another job failing, never fails a build, and is normal in passing builds. Jobs stopped by a failed dependency are `waiting_failed`, `blocked_failed` or `unblocked_failed` instead; those appear only in builds that actually failed and are consequences of an upstream failure, not root causes. None of these four states ran, so they have no logs. `failed` = ran and exited non-zero; `skipped` = an external factor (e.g. a newer build superseded it). To explain a red build, investigate only `failed`, `timed_out`, `expired` jobs that are not `soft_failed`, as well as `running` jobs that have non-zero `promised_exit_status`.

Soft failures: a job with `soft_failed` true actually ran and exited unsuccessfully, but the step's `soft_fail` setting allowed that exit status, so the failure did not block the build. `soft_fa… [truncated]

The queries this organization has certified, and results its members share on artifacts. Certify, uncertify, set up or share only when a person asked for exactly that. From a certified-query tool, org_disabled means certified queries are off for this organization: do not mention them or offer to certify or set up, and say they are off only if a person asks. Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. ## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (project-level units of work, each holding one PR-like Change per repository branch), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings. To create a trail for a branch, call trail_create with repo, title, body, branchName, and branchAction. For a trail web URL (…/-/trails/…), call project_trail action=get with url.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, entire/trails before trail work, entire/querying for the full querying reference. Load them proactively, at the start of the work, not after an error.

Feedback: if a tool is wrong, misleading, or missing something, call send_entire_feedback (name the tool). Code search is gated per jurisdiction — where the index is not deployed, those tools say so.

## claude.ai Linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

Tools accept human-readable references, so you rarely need to look up IDs first: issue identifiers such as LIN-123, project identifiers such as P-ENG-12, team names or keys, user names or emails, and "me" for the authenticated user. Only call list_teams, list_users, or similar tools when a reference is ambiguous or unknown.

Use list_issues for structured queries, such as the issues assigned to "me" in a team, status, label, project, or cycle, and its query parameter for keyword search. Results are paginated: when hasNextPage is true, pass the returned cursor to fetch the next page rather than assuming the first page is complete.

Statuses and labels belong to teams and differ between them. When you are not sure which values a team supports, call list_issue_statuses or list_issue_labels for that team before filtering or setting them.

get_issue does not include the issue's discussion. Call list_comments with the issue ID to read comments, including inline comments on the description.

Issue descriptions, comments, and documents often embed screenshots and other uploads as markdown images. Pass that markdown to extract_images to view them. Read issue attachments with get_attachment; files uploaded in comments are returned in the attachments field of list_comments. Linear upload URLs are signed and expire after a few minutes, so fetch them again instead of reusing old URLs.

Tools named save_* both create and update: omit id to create a new entity, or pass id to update an existing one. When updating, pass only the fields you want to change. To edit part of a long issue description or document, pass patch instead of resending the full content.

Before creating an issue, check with list_issues whether a matching issue already exists, to avoid duplicates. When creating, team is required.

The labels parameter of save_issue replaces the issue's full label set. To add or remove individual labels without dropping others, use addLabels and removeLabels instead.

Markdown content supports user mentions with @displayName (for example @johndoe). To embed an image or file, upload it with prepare_file_upload and insert the markdown it returns; do not inline base64 data.

Write issue descriptions for people to read. Keep sentences short, and use the same term for the same concept throughout.

Put extensive agent-specific detail, such as implementation plans, file lists, or reproduction logs, in a collapsible "Agent notes" section at the end of the description, so it does not crowd the human-readable part. A collapsible section opens with +++ followed by its title, and closes with +++ on its own line:

+++ Agent notes

Details for agents go here.

+++

[Alex]: I haven't been keeping up with the state-of-the-art in the CLI, what are `snapshots, fact-sets, overlays, manifests`? :sweat_smile:
[Alex]: @marvin can you help me out here?
[marvin (bot)]: Let me dig into the brain's own docs so I explain these accurately rather than guessing.Happy to help, @Alex! These four words are the "artifact kinds" the brain stores — they're the heart of Suhaan's trail 243 / PR #242. Here's the lay of the land.

*First, what "the brain" is:* it's Entire's Semantic Reasoning Layer — durable memory that agents read from and write to. Today it's local-only; this PR lifts it to a hosted, team-shared, multi-tenant service, wiring it onto the existing session-share stack (snapshotstore/snapshotcrypt/objstore), SpiceDB authz, and Postgres rather than standing up new infrastructure.

*The four artifact kinds.* The server store keys every brain artifact by `(repo_key, kind, ref)`, and `kind ∈ {snapshot, overlay, facts, manifest}` where `ref` is the content coordinate: commit for snapshot, `base..head` for overlay, branch for facts, commit for manifest. So, roughly:

• *snapshot* — the brain's state built at one specific commit (a full point-in-time capture). Keyed by that commit.
• *overlay* — an incremental delta layered on top, computed across a `base..head` range, so you don't rebuild the whole snapshot for every change. (M1 even adds a `brain_overlay_branches` migration for this.)
• *facts / fact-set* — the durable semantic facts, keyed by branch. This is the mutable one: M2 adds a CAS fact-set head plus a store-then-CAS `FactSetStore`, with two-member convergence, keep-both merge, provenance union, and conflict retry, backed by a tamper-evident hash-chained audit log. In plain terms — a shared, versioned set of "things we know" that multiple agents/people can advance concurrently without clobbering each other.
• *manifest* — the index/pointer describing which artifacts compose the brain at a given commit (the "table of contents"). Keyed by commit.
(The kind→coordinate mapping is straight from the brainstore PR #164; the "what each means" gloss is my reading of it — Suhaan's the ground truth if I've mischaracterised any.)

*One heads-up for the review itself:* this trail is big — four milestones (server store, fact-sync, remote MCP transport, and multi-tenancy) with four migrations `036`–`039`. So your instinct that it needs time to process is spot on. Might be worth reviewing milestone-by-milestone.

[Evis]: some thoughts after spending the day digging more into local -> hosted experience and the tools:

• there are generally 3 ways that developers can start localy:
    ◦ local developer with no repo yet on entire, no sessions or memory, starting from scratch
    ◦ local developer with a repo on entire, but no sessions or memory, starting from scrartch
    ◦ local developer with a repo on entire and with previous sessions from other teammates
• we need to think about all 3 paths and what the cold-start process looks like 
• i think the right way to think about the tooling is:
    ◦ semantic search finds relevant context from the transcripts and returns full checkpoints (s)
    ◦ brain helps retain and organize learned context and stored structured memories that can be retrieved locally and organized in a repo
    ◦ peregrine can retrieve code, symbols, and code locations across all repos quickly
    ◦ graph can add structural code relationships (need to see if this improves performance across our evals)
workflow i'm thinking about:
1. user installs entire CLI -> auto installs the brain plugin; entire identifies the local repository and if available the hosted repository, no sync happens yet
2. work locally -> memories are created locally as work is done. memories are useful locally across sessions, agents, etc. stored locally at this point
3. agent searches for memories -> call "context" api which returns memories, agent uses local and shared memories from hosted, we don't store hosted memories here
4. commit and push -> upload local memories in addition to transcripts and code. probably not embedded in the transcript, a part of the metadata.json file? im leaning towards a separate API
5. process memories -> reconcile duplicates, conflicts, (maybe we don't delete anything so we have full provenance), index, link to commits, transcripts, etc. and store somewhere
6. more local dev -> back to step 2
some open questions thinking about into the weekend:
• does memory grow indefinitely locally as local memories are created? do we prune? when? configurable?
• how do we reliably get the agent to use local tools and the hosted APIs instead of doing something else?
• how do we visualize these memories in the UI? is it a table? graph? should users be able to edit those memories in the UI as well?
• what happens if a memory gets corrected hosted but the old version is local? do we overwrite somehow and then reconcile locally by ID?
• do memories need any sort of scopes? can eveyrone see every memory? 
• what levels do memories live at? user? repo? project? org?
• how do we make sure we're not putting in conflicting memories? or if we do, how do we resolve those

• *overlay* — an incremental delta layered on top, computed across a `base..head` range, so you don't rebuild the whole snapshot for every change. (M1 even adds a `brain_overlay_branches` migration for this.)

In plain terms — a shared, versioned set of "things we know" that multiple agents/people can advance concurrently without clobbering each other.
• *manifest* — the index/pointer describing which artifacts compose the brain at a given commit (the "table of contents"). Keyed by commit.

[Evis]: some thoughts after spending the day digging more into local -> hosted experience and the tools:

• there are generally 3 ways that developers can start localy:
    ◦ local developer with no repo yet on entire, no sessions or memory, starting from scratch
    ◦ local developer with a repo on entire, but no sessions or memory, starting from scrartch
    ◦ local developer with a repo on entire and with previous sessions from other teammates
• we need to think about all 3 paths and what the cold-start process looks like 
• i think the right way to think about the tooling is:
    ◦ semantic search finds relevant context from the transcripts and returns full checkpoints (s)
    ◦ brain helps retain and organize learned context and stored structured memories that can be retrieved locally and organized in a repo
    ◦ peregrine can retrieve code, symbols, and code locations across all repos quickly
    ◦ graph can add structural code relationships (need to see if this improves performance across our evals)
workflow i'm thinking about:
1. user installs entire CLI -> auto installs the brain plugin; entire identifies the local repository and if available the hosted repository, no sync happens yet
2. work locally -> memories are created locally as work is done. memories are useful locally across sessions, agents, etc. stored locally at this point
3. agent searches for memories -> call "context" api which returns memories, agent uses local and shared memories from hosted, we don't store hosted memories here
4. commit and push -> upload local memories in addition to transcripts and code. probably not embedded in the transcript, a part of the metadata.json file? im leaning towards a separate API
5. process memories -> reconcile duplicates, conflicts, (maybe we don't delete anything so we have full provenance), index, link to commits, transcripts, etc. and store somewhere
6. more local dev -> back to step 2

• does memory grow indefinitely locally as local memories are created? do we prune? when? configurable?
• how do we reliably get the agent to use local tools and the hosted APIs instead of doing something else?
• how do we visualize these memories in the UI? is it a table? graph? should users be able to edit those memories in the UI as well?
• what happens if a memory gets corrected hosted but the old version is local? do we overwrite somehow and then reconcile locally by ID?
• do memories need any sort of scopes? can eveyrone see every memory? 
• what levels do memories live at? user? repo? project? org?

• *Continuous Memory* connects the semantic understanding of the codebase with the intent of the developer that created it, bringing the knowledge of the team together, learning from the experience and mistakes of past attempts, and compounding all that into better agent performance.
• *Consists of two components:*
    ◦ *Entire Graph:* installable plugin for the Entire CLI. It analyzes your repo and gives your agent a precomputed map of relevant code and relationships. Cuts token spend by up to 71%.
    ◦ *Entire Brain:* the memory layer for your repo, combining captured agent sessions and checkpoints with durable facts, documentation, and code understanding from *Entire Graph*. Because Brain sits in the repo rather than in one agent, Claude Code, Codex, or any agent Entire supports, all draw from the same memory source, and a session started in one agent is durable, continuous context for the next.

[marvin (bot)]: Let me dig into the brain's own docs so I explain these accurately rather than guessing.Happy to help, @Alex! These four words are the "artifact kinds" the brain stores — they're the heart of Suhaan's trail 243 / PR #242. Here's the lay of the land.

*First, what "the brain" is:* it's Entire's Semantic Reasoning Layer — durable memory that agents read from and write to. Today it's local-only; this PR lifts it to a hosted, team-shared, multi-tenant service, wiring it onto the existing session-share stack (snapshotstore/snapshotcrypt/objstore), SpiceDB authz, and Postgres rather than standing up new infrastructure.

*The four artifact kinds.* The server store keys every brain artifact by `(repo_key, kind, ref)`, and `kind ∈ {snapshot, overlay, facts, manifest}` where `ref` is the content coordinate: commit for snapshot, `base..head` for overlay, branch for facts, commit for manifest. So, roughly:

• *snapshot* — the brain's state built at one specific commit (a full point-in-time capture). Keyed by that commit.
• *overlay* — an incremental delta layered on top, computed across a `base..head` range, so you don't rebuild the whole snapshot for every change. (M1 even adds a `brain_overlay_branches` migration for this.)
• *facts / fact-set* — the durable semantic facts, keyed by branch. This is the mutable one: M2 adds a CAS fact-set head plus a store-then-CAS `FactSetStore`, with two-member convergence, keep-both merge, provenance union, and conflict retry, backed by a tamper-evident hash-chained audit log. In plain terms — a shared, versioned set of "things we know" that multiple agents/people can advance concurrently without clobbering each other.
• *manifest* — the index/pointer describing which artifacts compose the brain at a given commit (the "table of contents"). Keyed by commit.
(The kind→coordinate mapping is straight from the brainstore PR #164; the "what each means" gloss is my reading of it — Suhaan's the ground truth if I've mischaracterised any.)

    ◦ local developer with a repo on entire and with previous sessions from other teammates

    ◦ semantic search finds relevant context from the transcripts and returns full checkpoints (s)
    ◦ brain helps retain and organize learned context and stored structured memories that can be retrieved locally and organized in a repo
    ◦ peregrine can retrieve code, symbols, and code locations across all repos quickly
    ◦ graph can add structural code relationships (need to see if this improves performance across our evals)
workflow i'm thinking about:
1. user installs entire CLI -> auto installs the brain plugin; entire identifies the local repository and if available the hosted repository, no sync happens yet
2. work locally -> memories are created locally as work is done. memories are useful locally across sessions, agents, etc. stored locally at this point
3. agent searches for memories -> call "context" api which returns memories, agent uses local and shared memories from hosted, we don't store hosted memories here
4. commit and push -> upload local memories in addition to transcripts and code. probably not embedded in the transcript, a part of the metadata.json file? im leaning towards a separate API
5. process memories -> reconcile duplicates, conflicts, (maybe we don't delete anything so we have full provenance), index, link to commits, transcripts, etc. and store somewhere
6. more local dev -> back to step 2

Part of the [COR-2110](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2110/design-how-memories-attach-to-trails-upload-scope-triggers-edge-cases) design (v3) — see the design comment on [COR-2110](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2110/design-how-memories-attach-to-trails-upload-scope-triggers-edge-cases).

Replace branch-keyed set heads with per-fact storage:

* Rows keyed `(repo_id, fact_id)`, plus anchor rows per fact: SessionID, CheckpointID, Commit, TurnID. The synced blob already carries these (`SanitizeForEgress` strips only the local transcript path/line); today brainstore drops them. Branch may be kept as display metadata on an anchor, never as a key.
* Writes are idempotent upserts: anchors union, status advances one way (active → superseded/retracted), text/paths are fixed by the content-derived fact ID. Server stamps attribution from the token, as today.
* Endpoints: `POST /repos/{id}/brain/facts:upsert` (batch), `GET /repos/{id}/brain/facts?since=<cursor>` (repo-wide delta feed by `updated_at`, no branch parameter). Pagination is the platform standard — opaque cursor in, `next_cursor` out — implemented as a keyset over `(updated_at, fact_id)`, the same shape the `/memories` endpoint already uses; invent nothing new. Status changes bump `updated_at`, so retractions re-deliver through the same feed. Resync: omitting the cursor replays from zero (client applies are idempotent); a cursor predating a schema migration gets a reset error.
* A `trail_id` column, stamped on a fact when its trail merges (consume the trail-merge event; match the fact's anchors to the trail's membership) AND on upsert when an arriving fact's anchors belong to an already-merged trail — a session that ends after a squash merge uploads facts anchored to the trail's checkpoints, and the merge-time stamp alone would miss them, leaving them off the repo page forever. State: Backlog

**Repo:** entireio/entire-brain · From the 2026-11-06 command-surface survey.

## Problem

Brain no longer indexes code itself — `refresh index` states Graph owns the committed-tree index and shells out to `entire graph`. Yet Brain keeps 16 `inspect` verbs over its own `semstore` read layer (\~13k LOC across `semantic.go`, `semantic_graph.go`, `graph_store.go`, `internal/semstore`): `code`, `context`, `impact`, `search-graph`, `query-graph`, `graph-schema` (hidden), `graph-ui`, `snippet`, `trace-path`, `dead-code`, `ingest-traces`, `changes`, `tests`, `boundaries`, `regressions`, `blame`. `search-graph` is literally the same function as `inspect code` (`semantic_graph.go:412`). agentsetup already tells agents to use `entire graph query/def` directly.

## Change

Keep `context`, `impact`, and `tests` as thin delegations to `entire graph`; drop the rest. `graph-ui` goes with the separate browse-UI consolidation ticket. Precedent: [COR-2217](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2217/brain-delete-the-internal-semantic-read-path-keep-graceful-degradation) already deleted the internal semantic read path once — this finishes the job on the command surface.

## Acceptance

`inspect context|impact|tests` answer via Graph; removed verbs print a pointer to the `entire graph` equivalent for one release; `internal/semstore` consumers reduced to what the remaining verbs need.

Issue: ENT-1482 Investigate self-hosted embedding (and rerank) to replace Cohere API
State: Backlog

## Context

Search queries and indexing both call Cohere `embed-v4.0` ([api.cohere.com/v2](<http://api.cohere.com/v2>), internal/embedder/embedder.go), plus `rerank-v4.0-fast` at query time. Cohere rate limits are per API key (2,000 embed inputs/min, 1,000 rerank req/min) and forced the one-key-per-cell workaround (entire-search#142, infra#1030, fleet#3977). Motivation for this investigation: rate limits and reliability (e.g. 2026-07-21 429 storm), plus removing the external dependency and secret plumbing.

## Bedrock: investigated and ruled out (2026-08-03)

Checked live in the prod AWS account (934711778961) across all 4 cell regions:

* Cohere Embed v4 exists in all 4 regions but **inference-profile only** (no on-demand).
* ap-southeast-2 / ap-south-1 only have the `global.` profile → inference can route to any region worldwide (data residency problem) and defaults to 20 req/min.
* us-east-2 / eu-central-1 have regional `us.`/`eu.` profiles: 200 req/min, 300K tokens/min (vs ~1M TPM effective on the current Cohere key).
* **Non-adjustable 8.1M (cross-region) / 16.2M (global) tokens/DAY cap** — would make a full `--replace` backfill (CHUNK_VERSION-style) take weeks.
* rerank-v4.0-fast is not on Bedrock at all (only Rerank 3.5, eu-central-1 only).

Verdict: downgrade on every axis today. Re-check in 6–12 months. Near-term rate relief is a Cohere per-key limit increase or a sec

## Gap

We semantically index prose *about* code (commit subjects, PR titles/bodies, checkpoint transcript prose) but never the code changes themselves. Code retrieval is peregrine (trigram = exact token match). Commits with empty/lazy messages are unfindable semantically.

1. **Intent → implementation in one hop**: conceptual query lands on the diff hunk (with file/line), not just a transcript chunk that mentions it — removes the follow-up grep step.

===== linear_issue 2026-10-29 ENT-3664 [code-search] Query-tier LRU index cache over S3 (Phase 1: replace the full mirror) https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-3664/code-search-query-tier-lru-index-cache-over-s3-phase-1-replace-the
Issue: ENT-3664 [code-search] Query-tier LRU index cache over S3 (Phase 1: replace the full mirror)
State: Done

Make the peregrine query pod's index volume a bounded **LRU cache over S3** instead of a full mirror of the cell corpus. S3 stays the source of truth; indexes hydrate on first search and evict least-recently-searched.

**Spec:** `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-28-query-index-lru-cache-design.md`
**Plan:** `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-28-query-index-lru-cache-phase1.md`
(both committed in peregrine)

## Why now

The 2026-10-26 launch onboarding wave (\~50x repo-creation rate) pushed `data-peregrine-query-*` on eks-prod-us-east-2 from 60% to 83% in 42h. Resized 400Gi → 1Ti as an interim (fleet [entirehq/fleet#10622](https://linear.app/entirehq/review/peregrine-grow-us-east-2-query-pvc-template-400gi-1ti-e21799740772)). Under the full mirror, disk grows 1:1 with corpus on **every replica**, and every index build is re-downloaded by every replica.

Measured on the live prod volume (2026-10-28):

|  |  |
| -- | -- |
| Corpus on volume | 28,029 repos, 329.7GiB |
| **Ever searched in 111 days** | **903 repos, 31.4GiB — 3.2% of corpus** |
| Index churn | \~28k builds/day, \~2TB/day/replica downloaded |
| Query volume | \~100-200/day global |
| Query cost | p50 110ms, avg 250ms, p95 900ms on 2-CPU pods |
| Fan-out | median 4 repos, p95 154, max 253 (always account-scoped) |

Method: `/data` is mounted `relatime`, so an index whose `atime` is well past its `mtime` was read after it was written — i.e. searched. Re-runnable with `stat -c "%X %Y %s"` over `/data/indexes/*.pg`. It is a **lower bound** (relatime suppresses sub-24h updates; busy repos' mtime keeps refreshing), but the order of magnitude is solid: **96.8% of mirrored repos have never been searched once.**

148	Issue: ENT-3664 [code-search] Query-tier LRU index cache over S3 (Phase 1: replace the full mirror)
149	State: Done
150	
151	Make the peregrine query pod's index volume a bounded **LRU cache over S3** instead of a full mirror of the cell corpus. S3 stays the source of truth; indexes hydrate on first search and evict least-recently-searched.
152	
153	**Spec:** `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-28-query-index-lru-cache-design.md`
154	**Plan:** `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-28-query-index-lru-cache-phase1.md`
155	(both committed in peregrine)
156	
157	## Why now
158	
159	The 2026-10-26 launch onboarding wave (\~50x repo-creation rate) pushed `data-peregrine-query-*` on eks-prod-us-east-2 from 60% to 83% in 42h. Resized 400Gi → 1Ti as an interim (fleet [entirehq/fleet#10622](https://linear.app/entirehq/review/peregrine-grow-us-east-2-query-pvc-template-400gi-1ti-e21799740772)). Under the full mirror, disk grows 1:1 with corpus on **every replica**, and every index build is re-downloaded by every replica.
160	
161	Measured on the live prod volume (2026-10-28):
162	
163	|  |  |
164	| -- | -- |
165	| Corpus on volume | 28,029 repos, 329.7GiB |
166	| **Ever searched in 111 days** | **903 repos, 31.4GiB — 3.2% of corpus** |
167	| Index churn | \~28k builds/day, \~2TB/day/replica downloaded |
168	| Query volume | \~100-200/day global |
169	| Query cost | p50 110ms, avg 250ms, p95 900ms on 2-CPU pods |
170	| Fan-out | median 4 repos, p95 154, max 253 (always account-scoped) |
171	
172	Method: `/data` is mounted `relatime`, so an index whose `atime` is well past its `mtime` was read after it was written — i.e. searched. Re-runnable with `stat -c "%X %Y %s"` over `/data/indexes/*.pg`. It is a **lower bound** (relatime suppresses sub-24h updates; busy repos' mtime keeps refreshing), but the order of magnitude is solid: **96.8% of mirrored repos have never been searched once.**

===== linear_issue 2026-10-29 ENT-3664 [code-search] Query-tier LRU index cache over S3 (Phase 1: replace the full mirror) https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-3664/code-search-query-tier-lru-index-cache-over-s3-phase-1-replace-the
Issue: ENT-3664 [code-search] Query-tier LRU index cache over S3 (Phase 1: replace the full mirror)
State: Done

Make the peregrine query pod's index volume a bounded **LRU cache over S3** instead of a full mirror of the cell corpus. S3 stays the source of truth; indexes hydrate on first search and evict least-recently-searched.

**Spec:** `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-28-query-index-lru-cache-design.md`
**Plan:** `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-28-query-index-lru-cache-phase1.md`
(both committed in peregrine)

## Why now

The 2026-10-26 launch onboarding wave (\~50x repo-creation rate) pushed `data-peregrine-query-*` on eks-prod-us-east-2 from 60% to 83% in 42h. Resized 400Gi → 1Ti as an interim (fleet [entirehq/fleet#10622](https://linear.app/entirehq/review/peregrine-grow-us-east-2-query-pvc-template-400gi-1ti-e21799740772)). Under the full mirror, disk grows 1:1 with corpus on **every replica**, and every index build is re-downloaded by every replica.

Measured on the live prod volume (2026-10-28):

|  |  |
| -- | -- |
| Corpus on volume | 28,029 repos, 329.7GiB |
| **Ever searched in 111 days** | **903 repos, 31.4GiB — 3.2% of corpus** |
| Index churn | \~28k builds/day, \~2TB/day/replica downloaded |
| Query volume | \~100-200/day global |
| Query cost | p50 110ms, avg 250ms, p95 900ms on 2-CPU pods |
| Fan-out | median 4 repos, p95 154, max 253 (always account-scoped) |

Method: `/data` is mounted `relatime`, so an index whose `atime` is well past its `mtime` was read after it was written — i.e. searched. Re-runnable with `stat -c "%X %Y %s"` over `/data/indexes/*.pg`. It is a **lower bound** (relatime suppresses sub-24h updates; busy repos' mtime keeps refreshing), but the order of magnitude is solid: **96.8% of mirrored repos have never been searched once.**

# Why

/sessions runs two search systems and the client arbitrates between them per query (`SessionsPage.tsx`: `keywordSearchHealthy`): unscoped text goes to the search index (BM25 over transcripts + titles), but any facet/branch filter, index error, incomplete coverage, or empty response silently falls back to entire-api's PG substring search — which scans only name, first prompt, and agent (`store/sessions.go:916`). * Search **means something different depending on filter state**: add an author filter and transcript recall silently degrades to metadata substring.

Page lists have NO search bars: they are PG-backed browse views with facet filters only, plus an unadvertised Cmd+F "Find in view" text filter over already-loaded rows. **Repo:** entireio/entire-brain · **Phase C of the memories-only retrieval decision** (see [COR-2307](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2307/brain-brief-precedent-section-from-fact-provenance-anchors-not-history))

## Why

With memories as the only default retrieval surface, recall-time ranking quality carries the whole load. The 2026-11-06 retrieval audit found three concrete issues:

1. **Unresolved near-duplicates reach recall:** when distill judges two facts related below the old confidence threshold, both stay active cross-linked via `related_ids` (`factmerge/merge.go:40-46`). \~1,910 active records carry `related_ids`; pairs surface as separate results. Collapse linked facts into one result at recall time (newest or highest-scored wins, others listed as alternates). Complementary to [COR-2273](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2273/brain-nightly-memory-compaction-loop-merge-revise-retire) (nightly compaction, the storage-side fix) — recall-time collapse covers whatever compaction has not merged yet.
2. **No recency signal in recall:** the 90-day half-life recency weighting exists but only on `query` (`internal/cli/internal/retrieval/recency.go:66`, `retrieve.go:189`); `recall` never applies it. Add a default recency prior to recall.
3. **Flat +4 closed-negative bonus:** `facts_bm25.go:202-214` adds +4 to any closed-negative fact on any match, \~17% of the corpus, regardless of relevance. A recorded eval also found topically-similar closed-negatives out-competing the decision fact. Drop or justify the bonus.

## Constraint

Every ranking change goes through the offline eval harness (`memories eval`) before landing — recorde
